summary.text: Methanogens are anaerobic archaea that produce methane as a byproduct of their energy metabolism.
Making methane is their only way to generate ATP, and its enzymes are so sensitive to oxygen that they are exclusively anaerobic.
They live in wetlands, rice paddy soil, landfills, wastewater plants and animal digestive tracts, where they remove excess hydrogen and fermentation products.

facts.label: Deep ice find
facts.value: Live methane-makers found about three kilometres under Greenland

items.prompt: Why are methanogens mostly found in oxygen-free places rather than in open air?

options.label: Open air holds too much carbon dioxide for them
The enzymes in their methane pathway are extremely sensitive to oxygen
They can feed only on animal tissue
Their cells cannot survive above freezing

items.explain: Methanogens are exclusively anaerobic because of the extreme oxygen sensitivity of methanogenesis enzymes.

items.prompt: In an oxygen-free swamp, other microbes leave behind hydrogen and fermentation products. What do methanogens do with them?

options.label: Consume them, which clears the excess
Turn them into oxygen for the other microbes
Ignore them and feed on dead plants
Store them as fat for later

items.explain: In anaerobic environments methanogens remove excess hydrogen and fermentation products made by other microbes.

items.prompt: A student claims every methanogen is an extremophile. What is the better statement?

options.label: None are, because they all live in ordinary conditions
All are, because oxygen-free places count as extreme
Some are, but most live in ordinary conditions at near-neutral pH
Only those in animal guts are

items.explain: Some methanogens are extremophiles, but most isolates are mesophilic and grow around neutral pH, and most of their environments are not extreme.

items.prompt: A rover detects methane in the air of Mars. Why does that raise the possibility of life?

options.label: Only living animals are able to make methane
Methane is commonly generated by underground microbes such as methanogens
Methane is the gas that plants breathe in
Methanogens were already found in Martian rock samples

items.explain: Methane is commonly generated by underground microbes such as methanogens, so its detection signals a possibility of life.

items.prompt: A friend notes that some plants and animal cells also make methane, so they must be methanogens. Is that right?

options.label: Yes, any methane-making cell counts as a methanogen
Yes, as long as the cell lives without oxygen
No, because the methane they make is a different gas
No, in them the pathway differs and does not feed their energy supply

items.explain: All known methanogens belong to Archaea, and methane production in other organisms differs and does not contribute to ATP formation.

items.prompt: Most methanogens, unlike bacteria, lack a peptidoglycan wall. What do most have instead?

options.label: A protein array that fits together like a jigsaw puzzle
A thick shell of cellulose
A wall of chitin like that of fungi
A hard shell of silica

items.explain: Methanogens lack peptidoglycan, and most have a paracrystalline protein array, the S-layer, that fits together like a jigsaw puzzle.

paragraphs.heading: Archaea that make methane
paragraphs.text: Methanogens are archaea that give off methane as a by-product of their energy metabolism. Making methane, a process called methanogenesis, is their only biochemical route to ATP. Every known methanogen belongs to the domain Archaea. Some bacteria, plants and animal cells also release methane, but they use a different pathway, and it gives them no ATP.

paragraphs.heading: Life without oxygen
paragraphs.text: Methanogens are strictly anaerobic. The enzymes and iron-sulfur (FeS) clusters they use to make methane and ATP are extremely sensitive to oxygen, so the cells cannot work in aerobic conditions. Still, that sensitivity varies: methane making has often been detected in rice paddy soil that holds oxygen for a time. One wetland and soil species, Candidatus Methanothrix paradoxum, manages in small oxygen-free pockets inside aerobic surroundings, though even trace oxygen affects it. Methanosarcina barkeri stands out because it carries an enzyme called superoxide dismutase, and it may last longer than others when oxygen is present.

paragraphs.heading: Where they live
paragraphs.text: Methanogens are common in places with no oxygen: marine and freshwater sediments, wetlands, rice paddy soil, landfills, wastewater treatment plants and the digestive tracts of animals. They usually thrive once every electron acceptor except CO₂, such as oxygen, nitrate, ferric iron and sulfate, has run out. There they do an important ecological job, clearing away excess hydrogen and fermentation products made by other forms of anaerobic respiration. Most of these homes are not extreme, so the methanogens in them are not counted as extremophiles.

paragraphs.heading: Shapes and cell walls
paragraphs.text: More than 150 species have been described, and together they do not form a single branch of the archaeal family tree. Most are spheres, called cocci, or cylinders, called rods, though some grow as long filaments or curved forms. Like other archaea, they have no peptidoglycan, the polymer found in the cell walls of bacteria. Some build their wall from a material called pseudopeptidoglycan, also known as pseudomurein. Most, though, are wrapped in an S-layer, an orderly array of protein that fits together like a jigsaw puzzle.

paragraphs.heading: Extreme survivors
paragraphs.text: Some methanogens do live at extremes. Methanopyrus kandleri grows between 84 and 110 °C, and many well-studied methanogens, this one included, are thermophiles. Methanogens have also turned up in hot, dry desert soil and buried under kilometres of ice in Greenland. Researchers from the University of California, Berkeley found live methane makers in an ice core taken from about three kilometres below Greenland. Even so, most isolates are mesophilic and grow around neutral pH.

paragraphs.heading: In our guts and on Mars
paragraphs.text: The animal gut is rich in nutrients and mostly free of oxygen, which makes it a good home for methanogens. They were largely overlooked as gut residents until recently, yet they help keep the gut in balance by using up what bacterial fermentation leaves behind, such as H₂, acetate, methanol and methylamines. In the human gut the main methanogen is Methanobrevibacter smithii. Some scientists have even proposed that methane in the air of Mars could come from native methanogens there. In June 2019, NASA's Curiosity rover detected methane, a gas often made by underground microbes like these.
